newsitem.title: UK: UK trade figures warn of export problems ahead.
newsitem.headline: UK trade figures warn of export problems ahead.

text.p: A narrowing in the UK's trade deficit with the rest of the world suggests worries over the strong pound's effect on exporters are premature, but economists said the latest data suggest there will be problems ahead.
"There are warnings in these figures, in particular export volumes have fallen for the first time in a year," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"Added to the latest CBI survey showing export orders at a three year low, it suggests there are problems ahead."
Figures out on Wednesday showed the global deficit narrowed to 641 million pounds in January from 825 million pounds in December.
But export volumes fell by 0.5 percent in the three months to January after posting no new growth in the three months to December.
In the same period, imports volumes picked up pace, growing 2.5 percent compared with 1.0 percent in the three months to December.
"In a month or two I'm sure we'll see the deficit widen out as export volumes slow further," said Loynes.
The pound has gained around 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August.
British companies who rely heavily on exports have already made it clear their order books are thinning as a result and suggest it may not be long before output is hit.
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank of America, agreed that if these firms are finding it hard now, there could be worse to come.
"The numbers tend to fly in the face of some of the more pessimistic comments from UK firms, but some deterioration is likely as we move further into 1997."

More up-to-date figures also out on Wednesday showed the trade deficit with countries outside the Europe Union deteriorated in Februry. The deficit was 554 million pounds compared with 339 million in January. Exports managed to put in a better performance than the previous month. Exluding oil and eratics items, export volumes grew by 2.0 percent in the three months to February compared with 0.5 percent in the three months to January.
